finding.claim: Verifier cache ignores `exp` and `maxAge` for tokens that lack a numeric `iat`. A token that has an `exp` but no `iat` stays cached for the full `cacheTTL` (default 600000 ms) even after it expires. A cache hit returns the stored payload without re-checking expiry, so an expired token is accepted for up to 10 minutes past `exp`. The same applies to `nbf` on iat-less tokens. This is only exploitable when the issuer omits `iat`, for example via `noTimestamp`.
finding.source: A validly signed JWT that has `exp` but no `iat`, presented to a verifier with `cache` enabled. The attacker is a holder of such a token that has expired or been revoked.
finding.sink: Cache hit path in `verify` returns the cached payload via `handleCachedResult`, bypassing `verifyToken`'s exp validator.

trace.note: A successful verification calls cacheSet(cacheContext, payload).
`hasIat` is false when `iat` is missing, so the block that sets cacheValue[1] (nbf) and cacheValue[2] (exp) is skipped.
cacheValue[2] is 0, so it is set to `clockTimestamp + clockTolerance + cacheTTL`. The `exp` claim is never used to cap the TTL.
The next verification of the same token hits the cache. The `max` check passes until cacheTTL elapses, and `min` is 0.
The cached payload is returned without re-running `verifyToken`, so the `exp` check never runs.

finding.guards_checked: Checked `validateClaimDateValue`, which only runs on a cache miss. Checked the cache-hit time-range condition, which uses only the min/max values stored by `cacheSet`. Checked whether `exp` is applied when `iat` is absent: it is not. `cache` must be enabled, and it is off by default unless the `cache` option is set. I did not run this. I also have not compared the code with upstream fast-jwt, so this may be inherited behaviour rather than a local change.
